text: What would a pressure gauge above the liquid read as it warms and what must the molecules at the surface be doing to cause that?

I am studying why the vapor pressure of a liquid rises so steeply with temperature. Explain what the molecules at the surface are doing, using a liquid I have not named. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
In your own words what did the notebook show you about the molecules at the surface?
The problem is on your screen. Open the Equations list and pick the relation that expresses what you just described.
Which quantities in this problem were measured and which one is being inferred?

I need to recognise which equation links vapor pressure, temperature and heat of vaporization, in its two-point form and its straight-line form. Explain what each symbol stands for and when each form is the handy one. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What does each symbol in the relation you need stand for?
The relation is ln(P2/P1) = -(ΔHvap/R)(1/T2 - 1/T1); the straight-line form is ln P = -(ΔHvap/R)(1/T) + C.
Before any numbers go in: rearrange your relation so the quantity you are after stands alone on the left. Type it out.
Which quantity is the one you are after and what is the last operation standing between it and being alone?

Show me how to rearrange an equation that has a natural log on one side and a difference of reciprocal temperatures on the other so that a chosen variable stands alone. Use symbols different from mine and do not use my numbers. Then give me one short practice rearrangement and wait for my answer.
What operation undoes a natural log and what undoes a reciprocal?
What must be true of a temperature before it can go into this relation? Convert and type the kelvin value(s).
What would it mean for the molecules if a temperature of zero on your scale were put into 1/T?
Explain why gas-law and vapor-pressure equations need absolute temperature, using an example I have not named. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait.
Why does this relation need an absolute temperature?
Add 273.15 to each Celsius temperature to get kelvin.
Look at the units of R and of the heat of vaporization. What has to happen before they meet in one fraction? Convert one of them and type the value with its unit.
What units must ΔHvap/R end up with for the equation to balance?
Explain how to keep energy units consistent between the gas constant R and a heat of vaporization given in kJ/mol. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What did you find about the units of R and ΔHvap?
Either multiply ΔHvap in kJ/mol by 1000 to get J/mol or use R = 0.008314 kJ/(mol K).
The two pressures sit in one ratio. What must be true of their units? Convert one and type it.
What should the units of P2/P1 be?
Explain why two pressures in a ratio must share a unit and how atm, torr and kPa relate. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What must be true of two pressures before you divide one by the other?
1 atm = 760 torr = 101.325 kPa. Put both pressures in the same unit.
Put your measured values into the relation and show me what you get for each side.
Which of your numbers came from an instrument and which are you about to infer?
Show me how to substitute values into the two-point vapor pressure relation and isolate an unknown, using numbers and a liquid different from mine. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What is the first thing you will do with your numbers now?
Substitute the kelvin temperatures and the matched pressures and keep ΔHvap and R in matching units. Then isolate the unknown.
Carry it through. What value do you get and in what units?
Before you calculate should the answer be larger or smaller than the value you were given and why?

Explain how to isolate an unknown from an equation with a natural log on one side and reciprocal temperatures on the other, using an example different from mine. Then ask me one short question and wait.
Which step of the algebra was blocking you?
Isolate the unknown: exponentiate both sides for a pressure; solve for 1/T and take the reciprocal for a temperature.
Before any numbers: write ΔHvap in terms of the slope of your line. Type the equation with ΔHvap alone on the left.
Set your straight line beside the relation you picked. Which group of symbols sits where the slope sits?

Show me how to rearrange a straight-line equation of the form ln(y) = m(1/x) + b for a chosen variable, and how a slope can stand for a physical quantity. Use symbols different from mine and no numbers of mine. Then give me one short practice rearrangement and wait for my answer.
Which part of the relation plays the part of the slope?
What does the slope of your line stand for and what heat of vaporization does it give? Type the value with its unit.
If the line were steeper what would that say about how hard it is for a molecule to leave the liquid?
Explain how the slope of a plot of ln P against 1/T gives the heat of vaporization, using data different from mine. Do not solve my problem. Then ask me one short question and wait.
How does the slope connect to the heat of vaporization?
Slope = -ΔHvap/R so ΔHvap = -(slope)(R).
Now rearrange your line so that T stands alone on the left. Type it.
What would the gauge read at the normal boiling point and where does that reading go in your line?

Show me how to rearrange a straight-line equation of the form ln(y) = m(1/x) + b for a chosen variable, and how a slope can stand for a physical quantity. Use symbols different from mine and no numbers of mine. Then give me one short practice rearrangement and wait for my answer.
What undoes a reciprocal and in what order do you clear the terms around 1/T?
What defines the normal boiling point and where is that on your line? Type the temperature with its unit.
What would a pressure gauge read above the liquid at the moment it boils in an open beaker at sea level?

Explain what the normal boiling point means in terms of vapor pressure and how to find it from a straight-line fit of ln P against 1/T, using data different from mine. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What condition defines the normal boiling point?
Set P to 760 torr in your line and solve for T.
Look back at your result. What does it let you claim about molecules you never saw and how sure can you be?
What did the instrument actually measure and what did you infer from it?
Help me think about what a vapor pressure measurement lets a chemist infer about molecules in the liquid and what it cannot. Do not give me a finished answer. Ask me one short question and wait.
What is the difference between what was measured and what was inferred?
A pressure gauge inside the syringe would read lower after you pull the plunger. What does that lower pressure let the water molecules do?

I am learning why a liquid can boil without being heated. Explain what the molecules in a liquid are doing when it boils. Explain why lowering the pressure above a liquid can make it boil. Use a liquid other than water. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
In your own words, what did the notebook show you about why lower pressure lets a liquid boil?
When the pressure on a liquid drops to its vapor pressure, molecules inside the liquid can form bubbles of vapor. The liquid boils. No heat is needed.
Before any math, compare the two temperatures. Will the pressure you are finding be higher or lower than the pressure you were given? Pick one.
Think about the molecules at the surface. At the lower of your two temperatures, do more or fewer of them have enough energy to escape?

I need to predict how the vapor pressure of a liquid changes when its temperature changes, before I calculate anything. Explain what the molecules are doing and which way the pressure goes. Use a liquid I have not named. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
What did the notebook show you about temperature and vapor pressure?
Vapor pressure goes up when temperature goes up. It goes down when temperature goes down. In a cooler liquid, fewer molecules have enough energy to escape.
The pressure you found is the pressure inside the syringe at the moment the liquid starts to boil. What does it tell you about the molecules? How sure can you be?
We used one value of ΔHvap for every temperature between your two temperatures. If that is not quite true, how far can you trust the pressure you found?
Which step was hardest for you? In one sentence, what would you tell a friend who is stuck there?
A thermometer on the wet head reads a few degrees colder than one on the body. What does the colder glass do to the molecules inside the head?

I am learning how a drinking bird toy works. Explain what water molecules do when they evaporate from a wet surface. Then explain why a sealed glass container that is cool at one end and warm at the other has a different vapor pressure at each end. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
In your own words, what did the notebook show you about the two ends of the bird?
Water evaporating from the felt cools the head. Inside the glass, the cooler head has a lower vapor pressure than the warm body. The higher pressure in the body pushes liquid up the neck.
Now compare the two ends of the bird. How much higher is the pressure in the body than in the head? Type the difference with its unit.
You have the pressure in the warm body and the pressure in the cool head. Which is larger, and by how much?

I need to find the difference between two vapor pressures in a sealed container that is warm at one end and cool at the other. Explain what that difference means and how to find it. Use numbers different from mine. Do not solve my problem. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
What does the difference between the two pressures tell you?
Subtract: the pressure in the body minus the pressure in the head.
That difference pushes liquid up the neck. Think of drinking through a straw. In the bird, what acts like your mouth, and what acts like the air pushing down on the drink?
Inside the cool head, what are the vapor molecules doing that the ones in the warm body are not?
Carry it through to the pressure you are finding. If you have the ln (natural logarithm) of a pressure ratio, what undoes ln? Type the pressure with its unit.
Look at the prediction pinned on your screen. Does your number agree with it?
Show me how to solve an equation like ln(x/a) = b for x. Use letters and numbers different from mine. Do not solve my problem. Then give me one short practice problem and wait for my answer.
What undoes ln (natural logarithm)? And what do you do after that to get the pressure you are finding?
Undo the ln: e raised to the other side gives the ratio of the two pressures. Then solve that ratio for the pressure you are finding.
A pressure gauge at the vent reads far higher than at the surface. What must the molecules inside a bubble do to push back against that?

I am learning why very hot water on the deep sea floor does not boil. Explain what molecules must do to form a bubble of vapor inside a liquid. Explain how the pressure on the liquid changes that. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
In your own words, what did the notebook show you about pressure and bubbles?
A bubble forms only when the vapor inside it pushes back as hard as the liquid around it. Deep water presses hard, so the water must be much hotter before it can boil.
Before any math, compare the two pressures. Will the temperature you are finding be higher or lower than the temperature you were given? Pick one.
Think about a bubble trying to form. Under more pressure, do the molecules need more energy or less to push it open?

I need to predict how the boiling point of a liquid changes when the pressure on it changes, before I calculate anything. Explain what the molecules are doing and which way the boiling point goes. Use a liquid I have not named. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
What did the notebook show you about pressure and boiling point?
Boiling point goes up when the pressure goes up. The molecules need more energy to push a bubble open.
How hard does the water press at the vent? Use the depth to find the pressure. Type it with its unit.
Picture the column of water above the vent. Each 10 m of it adds about 1 atm. What does the air above the sea add?

Explain how the pressure under water grows with depth, and why the air above the water counts too. Use a depth different from mine. Do not solve my problem. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
What did the notebook show you about pressure and depth?
Pressure = 1 atm from the air + 1 atm for every 10 m of water.
Carry it through to the temperature. If you have 1/T, what is one more step? Type the temperature with its unit.
Look at the prediction pinned on your screen. Does your number agree with it?

Show me how to solve an equation like 1/x = a - b for x, and how to check that the answer makes sense. Use numbers different from mine. Do not solve my problem. Then give me one short practice problem and wait for my answer.
What is the last step to get T from 1/T?
Solve for 1/T first. Then take the reciprocal: T = 1 ÷ (your value of 1/T). Convert to °C if the problem asks for it.
Your temperature is where water starts to boil at that depth. What does it tell you about the water molecules there? How sure can you be?
We used water's heat of vaporization at 100 °C for every temperature up to yours. How far can you trust the answer at great depth?
At the same temperature, a vapor monitor reads much higher over the alcohol than over the water. What does that tell you about how strongly each kind of molecule holds on to its neighbors?

I am learning why some liquids evaporate faster than others at the same temperature. Explain it in terms of the attractions between molecules. Use liquids other than alcohol and water. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
In your own words, what did the notebook show you about why one liquid evaporates faster than another?
Molecules that hold on to their neighbors less strongly escape into vapor more easily. More of them leave each second, so the liquid dries faster and carries more heat away from your skin.
Carry it through to ΔHvap. Type the value with its unit.
Does your answer make sense? Most liquids in our table need 25 to 45 kJ/mol to vaporize. Is yours in that range?
Show me how to solve an equation like ln(a) = -(x/R)(b - c) for x. Use numbers different from mine. Do not solve my problem. Then give me one short practice problem and wait for my answer.
Which step of the algebra was blocking you?
Divide ln(P2/P1) by (1/T2 - 1/T1). Multiply by -R. Give ΔHvap in kJ/mol.
Your ΔHvap is the energy it takes to pull a mole of the liquid's molecules away from their neighbors and into vapor. What does your number tell you about those molecules? How sure can you be?
What did the instrument actually measure and what did you infer from it?
